System Design · PS 28 · Feasibility Report

Low-Latency Distributed Feature Flag Service

Virtual Lab and Simulator — demonstrating local feature-flag evaluation and asynchronous configuration updates.

Client-side evaluation · Control plane · Simulation
01

Executive Summary

The Low-Latency Distributed Feature Flag Service virtual lab is feasible as a course project. It is an interactive, browser-based simulator, not a production service.

It can be built from well-understood parts: a React user interface, a TypeScript simulation engine with capacities, an SVG architecture canvas, a mobile app preview and an automated test suite.

The main design idea is the separation of two paths. The hot evaluation path runs fully inside the client from an in-memory cache and needs no network call. The cold configuration path carries admin changes through a configuration service, cloud storage, a Pub/Sub broker and an SSE server to the clients. Because the two paths are independent, a failure in storage, broker or streaming server does not stop flag evaluation.

The main costs of the project are the effort to model the 10 components correctly and the risk that modelled numbers are mistaken for real measurements. The tools are free and no cloud infrastructure is needed.

Recommendation: proceed with the project. All performance figures must be reported as modelled values produced by the simulation engine, not as benchmarks measured on physical hardware.
02

Introduction and Problem Statement

Feature flags (also called feature toggles) let a team switch a feature on or off without releasing new code. They support gradual rollouts, canary releases, A/B experiments and emergency kill switches. Large applications such as e-commerce sites, streaming services and social networks check flags thousands of times every second, so the way a flag is evaluated has a direct effect on speed and reliability.

In a naive design, every flag check is a remote call (HTTP or RPC) to a central flag service or database. This design has three serious problems:

  1. Latency overhead: A remote call takes about 20 to 150 ms depending on distance, TLS handshakes and database load. Adding this to the checkout or page-rendering path hurts the user experience.
  2. Single point of failure: If the central service or the network link goes down, the client application stalls or crashes while it waits for a timeout.
  3. Database exhaustion: An application that serves 50,000 requests per second would send 50,000 queries per second to the configuration database just to read static boolean values.

High-performance systems such as LaunchDarkly and Split.io avoid these problems with a decoupled dual-path design. Flags are evaluated locally from an in-memory cache inside an SDK embedded in the client (the data plane). Changes made by an administrator are stored, published and pushed to the clients in the background (the control plane).

This report asks whether a virtual lab that demonstrates this design can be built within the course timeframe, whether its costs are justified, and what the simulator can credibly show.

03

Project Objectives

  1. Show clearly that local flag evaluation is separate from background configuration updates.
  2. Model 10 architectural components, including load, utilization, latency, throughput, dropped requests and component health.
  3. Provide an interactive mobile app preview (ShopEasy) whose screen changes according to the flag value received by the Client SDK.
  4. Allow controlled fault injection (storage failure, broker failure, SSE failure, cache or SDK failure, traffic spike and network delay).
  5. Demonstrate eventual consistency and the stale-cache fallback: clients keep evaluating flags from the cache while updates are blocked.
  6. Verify the design rules with an automated acceptance test suite.

Scope

In scope: browser-based simulation engine, interactive SVG architecture canvas with animated flows and health indicators, live charts of modelled load, throughput and latency, ShopEasy phone preview, component capacity tuning, fault injection, event log, four preset scenarios and acceptance checks.

Out of scope: physical cloud servers (AWS or GCP), real Kafka or Redis brokers, a real relational or NoSQL database, real network sockets, user authentication, role-based access control, multiple flags, targeting rules or persistent storage. These are future work.

Assumptions

  • The system runs inside a browser tab. Distributed components and their behaviour are represented by a simulation rather than deployed infrastructure.
  • The simulation advances in steps of one second.
  • The simulator has a single flag, new_checkout, and a single phone client.
  • Component capacities and base latencies are fixed starting values (for example 6,000 req/s for the Evaluation Engine and 4,000 push/s for the SSE server). The user can tune the capacities.
  • The cache hit ratio is assumed to be 99.8% when the cache is healthy and not overloaded.
04

System Overview

The system is organised in three zones. The Configuration Control Plane manages, stores and propagates flag changes. The Client-Side Evaluation Zone (data plane) evaluates flags in memory. The Monitoring Zone collects telemetry without blocking evaluations.

Configuration Service→Cloud Configuration Storage→Pub/Sub Broker→SSE Update Server→Client SDK→Local Flag Cache
Client Instances→Load Generator→Client SDK→Local Flag Cache→SDK Evaluation Engine

The evaluation path never calls the control-plane components.

Component Responsibilities

ComponentZoneCapacityBase latencyResponsibility
Client InstancesEvaluation12,000 req/s0.1 msApps, browsers and services that send flag evaluation requests
Load GeneratorEvaluation10,000 req/s0.2 msCreates the traffic and models high incoming traffic
Client SDKEvaluation8,000 req/s0.3 msEmbedded library that reads the cache, runs evaluations and listens for updates
Local Flag Cache (L1)Evaluation12,000 req/s0.2 msIn-memory hash table with O(1) flag lookup
SDK Evaluation EngineEvaluation6,000 req/s0.5 msApplies rules and returns ON, OFF or a variant
Configuration ServiceControl plane500 req/s8.0 msAdmin API to create, validate and toggle flags
Cloud Configuration StorageControl plane400 req/s15.0 msDurable store for the latest flag state, versions and audit history
Pub/Sub BrokerControl plane2,500 ev/s5.0 msPublishes flag update events and decouples producer from consumer
SSE Update ServerControl plane4,000 push/s4.0 msKeeps persistent connections and pushes updates to clients
Monitoring and TelemetryMonitoring2,000 req/s2.0 msCollects 5% sampled metrics, cache hit ratio and latency data

Capacities and latencies are starting values in the simulator, and the user can change the capacity of any component.

What is implemented and what is simulated

The browser interface, architecture canvas, ShopEasy preview, charts, event log and fault controls are implemented. The ten architecture components represent simulated services. Load, utilization, latency, throughput and errors are modelled values, not hardware measurements. The test suite is described in the project context, but its latest execution result has not been independently verified.

Modelling approach

The simulator compares incoming traffic with each component’s configured capacity. Utilization describes how busy a component is relative to its capacity. At high traffic, the model shows capacity saturation, limited successful throughput and possible dropped requests. Latency represents the modelled time needed for a component or an update path; it is not measured from a live distributed deployment.

Consistency and failure handling

The update is first written to storage, and only then published. If storage fails, the update is aborted. If the broker or the SSE server fails, the value stays saved but the clients keep their cached value, and the status shows as blocked. After recovery the lab synchronises the client again. This models eventual consistency without any distributed coordination code.

Implementation note: Performance numbers can look like measurements even though they come from the simulator. P95 is a heuristic estimate rather than a measured percentile. The healthy, non-overloaded cache hit assumption is 99.8%, not a measured result.
06

Operational Feasibility

The lab is easy to operate. It is a static web application that opens in any modern browser from the live link. The user needs no installation, account or server.

How the lab is used

  • Students change the request rate, number of concurrent clients and network delay with sliders, or choose a preset load (Low 250, Normal 1,500, High 4,500 or Overload 8,500 req/s).
  • The admin toggle changes the new_checkout flag. The ShopEasy phone preview switches between the traditional card-entry checkout and the 1-click checkout when the update reaches the SDK.
  • Four ready scenarios (Normal, Traffic Spike, Pub/Sub Failure, Storage Failure) show the main behaviours in one click.
  • The Component Inspector lets the user fail or restore any component and tune its capacity from 200 to 15,000 req/s.
  • A Reset button restores the default state at any time.

What the lab monitors: The interface presents modelled latency, throughput, error rate, cache hit ratio, update propagation time and component health using charts, utilization indicators and the event log. These values help students compare scenarios; they are not real infrastructure telemetry.

Maintenance: There is no server to monitor or patch. Updating the lab means rebuilding and redeploying the static site. State is kept in memory, so a page refresh resets the simulator. This is acceptable for a teaching and demonstration tool.

Users: The intended users are computer science and system design students, and evaluators in a viva who want to inspect failures, bottlenecks and recovery without paying for cloud services.

07

Economic Feasibility

The project is economically feasible because it uses only free and open-source tools and does not deploy any paid infrastructure. A production feature flag service would require ongoing spending on hosting, storage, messaging and monitoring. This virtual lab demonstrates the architectural trade-offs without deploying those services.

Local evaluation can reduce dependence on remote lookups, but this simulator does not establish a monetary saving or production break-even point. The economic comparison is qualitative: a production team would weigh faster local evaluations and improved resilience against SDK maintenance, update delivery and infrastructure costs.

10

Acceptance Criteria and Evaluation Plan

Acceptance Criteria

  1. Toggling the flag changes the admin value, and when the update path is healthy the phone client receives the same value.
  2. When the Pub/Sub broker is failed, the phone stays on the cached value, the status shows as blocked, and after recovery the client synchronises to the new value.
  3. Evaluation traffic reaches only the hot-path components. Cloud Storage, the broker and the SSE server see only idle or update load (2 to 5 req/s).
  4. When offered traffic exceeds the Evaluation Engine’s configured capacity, its modelled utilization reaches its limit and successful throughput cannot continue increasing at the same rate. The simulator may show dropped requests under overload.
  5. During control-plane failures, cached evaluation can continue while the SDK, local cache and evaluation engine remain healthy and sufficient capacity is available. This is an expected model behaviour, not a universal zero-error guarantee.
  6. The update propagation latency is a deterministic model value of 32.5 ms (modelled) at 0 ms network delay and 72.5 ms at 40 ms network delay.
  7. When concurrent clients exceed the simulated SSE server capacity, update delivery may be affected. No specific waiting-broadcast count or delay is asserted here.
  8. Reset restores the default state with all 10 components healthy.

The project context describes 14 grouped acceptance checks in the test suite. Their current pass status must be confirmed from a recent test execution before being reported as a verified result. The acceptance checks cover local evaluation, configuration updates, failures, capacity limits and reset behaviour. Their expected outcomes are model behaviours rather than measurements on physical servers.

Metrics

The lab reports modelled performance metrics. Utilization means how much of a component’s available processing capacity is being used. Throughput means how many evaluation requests the model successfully handles per second. Latency means the modelled time taken to complete an evaluation or deliver an update. Error rate describes the share of offered requests that the model cannot successfully process. Cache hit ratio describes how often the simulated local lookup finds a flag value.

At a moderate request rate, a component may operate below its capacity and serve requests normally. When demand becomes greater than its configured capacity, the simulator can show saturation and reduced successful service.

P95 latency is a heuristic estimate calculated by the simulator. It is not the 95th percentile of observed network requests or hardware timings. The healthy cache hit ratio of 99.8% is a simulation assumption.

Modelled throughput is constrained by the relevant evaluation components. If the SDK, cache or evaluation engine is marked failed, evaluation cannot proceed. The normal evaluation latency of about 1.3 ms and configuration propagation latency of 32.5 ms are baseline model values, not real benchmark results.

Test Scenarios

ScenarioSettingExpected result
Normal operation1,500 req/s, 1,000 clients, 0 ms delayAll components healthy, evaluation about 1.3 ms, flag reaches the phone in 32.5 ms.
Traffic spike7,500 req/sEvaluation Engine (6,000 req/s) saturates, queue fills, error rate and latency rise, control plane stays at about 2 req/s.
Pub/Sub failureBroker failed, flag toggledPhone shows stale value with an Update Blocked badge, evaluations continue at 1,500 evals/s with 0 errors, client syncs after recovery.
Storage failureCloud Storage failed, flag toggledToggle fails with HTTP 503 and the phone keeps the cached flag.
SSE failureSSE server failedUpdate blocked, hot path unaffected, backlog pushed after restore.
Cache or SDK failureCache or SDK failedThroughput drops to 0 and error rate becomes 100% until restored.
11

Limitations and Future Scope

Limitations

  1. Simulation, not infrastructure: The lab does not measure real CPU instructions or network packets. It does not use a real database, Kafka, Redis or EventSource connections.
  2. Memory-only state: A page refresh returns the simulator to its defaults.
  3. Single flag: Only new_checkout exists, so multi-flag bucketing and flag dependencies cannot be studied.
  4. Synthetic tail latency: The P95 value is a heuristic estimate rather than a measured percentile from real requests.
  5. Assumed cache hit ratio: The 99.8% hit ratio is assumed for healthy ticks; the displayed value uses accumulated simulated hits and misses, not actual user lookups.
  6. No security features: User authentication and role-based access control are not implemented.

Future Scope

  1. Save flags and tuned capacities in the browser (localStorage or IndexedDB) so they survive a reload.
  2. Add a lightweight backend with real REST endpoints and real Redis Pub/Sub.
  3. Add a real SSE gateway (EventSource) so that several browser tabs act as independent client SDKs.
  4. Add a targeting engine with percentage rollouts based on a hash of the user ID and user attribute rules.
12

Conclusion and Recommendation

The Low-Latency Distributed Feature Flag Service virtual lab is technically, operationally and economically feasible as a course prototype.

It uses free tools, runs fully in the browser and demonstrates the central design idea: flag evaluation stays on a fast in-memory path, while configuration updates travel on a separate asynchronous path.

The main risks are modelling accuracy and misleading interpretation of simulated values. These are addressed through clearly defined acceptance checks, review of the simulation logic and consistent labelling of modelled results; independent test execution evidence should be retained.

Recommendation: use the project as an educational virtual lab. Results should be presented as modelled outcomes, with the limitations explained clearly and without implying production deployment.
